SourceNumberedExerciseLedger.SourceTeacherExpectedMath: A polynomial has only nonnegative integer powers; a rational function is p(x)/q(x), with q a nonzero polynomial. Every polynomial may also be written over denominator 1.
Polynomial graphs are continuous on all real x, while rational graphs can have vertical asymptotes or removable discontinuities where the original denominator vanishes.
Numerator and denominator share a factor whose zero is cancelled algebraically, but remains excluded from the original domain.
Yes. A denominator may have no real roots (such as x²+1), or all its real zero factors may cancel to produce holes rather than vertical asymptotes.
Yes. The numerator may have no real roots, or all its real roots may be removed by original denominator restrictions.

One vertical asymptote; left branch falls toward minus infinity and right branch descends from positive infinity, crossing x-axis at positive input.
Two vertical asymptotes; middle branch is below x-axis except at a tangent contact, indicating an even-multiplicity zero; outer branches separated.
Two vertical asymptotes; middle branch touches x-axis at a local minimum and rises on both sides; compare denominator sign and repeated zero.
